Dear Secretary Reese:

        The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), through this filing,
submits this informational report in compliance with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s
(the “Commission”) Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act
issued in this proceeding on June 18, 2026 (the “Show Cause Order”).1 MISO respectfully requests
that the Commission accept this filing in compliance with the Show Cause Order’s requirements.

I.         Executive Summary

         MISO appreciates the support of the Commission to ensure efficient, cost-effective and
reliable integration of large loads. MISO continues to work diligently with the states both
individually and through the Organization of MISO States (“OMS”), as well as its member
utilities, to support resource adequacy for planned load growth in a manner that maintains customer
affordability, efficiency and regional reliability. MISO’s current framework is well-suited to meet
the needs of traditional load growth, and MISO’s existing processes have enabled us to maintain
resource adequacy. The unique nature of certain new large loads and the need to help ensure speed
to power, however, brings new challenges that require MISO to continue to work with its states
and broader stakeholder community to develop new tools and processes to ensure resource
adequacy is maintained going forward. Conventional load forecasting was designed around
gradual and geographically-dispersed growth. The new large loads, which include data center
developments, reflect a new type of load growth. A single project may require more load than an
entire city at one location and desire service within a short period. This concentrated and
discontinuous load growth requires new processes to most effectively meet this new demand and
maintain resource adequacy. Many of these new large loads are difficult to forecast with a high

not align well with traditional utility planning. It is not prudent for load serving entities to build
local transmission, or generation, for speculative loads. Yet the pace of large load additions and
early need-by dates nonetheless require acceleration of transmission planning and generator
interconnection processes, even in the face of this uncertainty.

        While MISO’s existing processes have been sufficient to ensure resource adequacy in the
short term, the unique operational characteristics of new large loads have prompted MISO to
consider new processes within the current regulatory framework and Resource Adequacy
construct. As discussed below, MISO, the states, and our members have taken a number of steps
to address resource adequacy in the near term and to plan for resource adequacy needs in the future
given the shifting resource mix and risk profile in the MISO region.

        In order to meet the unique speed to power needs of these new large loads and provide
additional tools that support resource adequacy, MISO is developing two new processes to speed
the delivery of energy to large loads. First, MISO will file its Zero Injection Generator
Interconnection Agreement (“ZGIA”) by early August. MISO began working with stakeholders
in 2025 to develop a new Interconnection service study type—ZG Interconnection Service, an
associated study process, and revisions to its pro forma Generator Interconnection Agreement and
modifications to its pro forma GIA designed to facilitate faster interconnection of generation
resources that serve only Load connected to the same substation and will not inject energy further
onto the Transmission System. As discussed in more detail below, the ZGIA is not restricted to
use only for large loads. However, the process is particularly responsive to the challenges faced
by large loads. The ZGIA will facilitate the accelerated interconnection of generation needed to
serve a specific nearby load source where broader injection onto the broader Transmission System
is not needed and system impacts—and corresponding Network Upgrades—can be limited to
roughly the substation level. This provides a valuable option for generation to be co-located with
large loads without having enter the Definitive Planning Phase of MISO’s generation
interconnection queue or obtain a form of Interconnection Service that is broader and potentially
more costly than what is needed.

        In addition, at the July 16, 2026 Large Load Working Group MISO initiated stakeholder
discussions to develop a new set of processes for concurrently studying large loads and associated
generation.2 This new framework (provisionally named the “Large Load Parallel Study Process”)
aligns the study processes used to assess the transmission infrastructure needed to meet new large
loads and new generation in an efficient framework that can be executed on a shorter timeline
using shared modelling inputs. The Large Load Parallel Study Process recognizes the unique
commercial realities of these new large loads. This framework is expected to position MISO’s
members to meet the challenges presented by new large loads on a more immediate timeline. The
Large Load Parallel Study Process will support resource adequacy and further supplement the
opportunities available for members to effectively facilitate new large spot loads, with speed, and
supports resource adequacy while protecting customers from unnecessary investments relating to

II.        BACKGROUND

        On June 18, 2026, the Commission issued the Show Cause Order. The Show Cause Order
directed the following compliance requirements:

                       122. Accordingly, we direct MISO to submit in Docket No. EL26-
                       70-000, within 30 days of the date of issuance of this order, a
                       detailed informational report on any proposals under consideration
                       in its stakeholder process to address the issue of resource adequacy
                       to serve new large loads. We also strongly encourage new proposals
                       to the extent necessary to address these concerns. The informational
                       report must include a detailed schedule of key milestones, such as
                       stakeholder or MISO Board votes, that includes the estimated date
                       on which MISO expects to file any such proposals with the
                       Commission. Additionally, as part of this informational report, we
                       direct MISO to identify any ongoing stakeholder processes that aim
                       to increase the pace of adding generating capacity in the MISO
                       region. The informational report must include a detailed schedule
                       of such initiatives, including timing of the stakeholder process and
                       dates of any anticipated filings with the Commission.3

III.       INFORMATIONAL FILING

        To respond to the Show Cause Order’s requirements, MISO has divided its informational
report into three sections. Sections A and B discuss MISO’s role in promoting Resource Adequacy
in the MISO Region and the ability of the Transmission System to meet projected large load
demands under current Tariff processes and expected generation additions. Section C discusses
new initiatives that MISO is developing with its stakeholders to further buttress resource adequacy
and accelerate the pace of adding generation to meet the emerging needs of large loads.

           A.          The MISO Region Is Resource Adequate.

                       1.     The role of the States in ensuring resource adequacy.

       Within the MISO region, States are primarily responsible for resource adequacy, which
involves overseeing Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”) and ensuring LSEs plan for and secure enough
power to meet their customers’ demand. MISO supports resource adequacy by determining
Planning Reserve Margin, administering the Planning Resource Auction and providing data for
planning, but it is the responsibility of the States and LSEs to ensure sufficient capacity is available

to meet Load and reserve requirements. MISO’s Resource Adequacy construct complements the
jurisdiction that State commissions and Relevant Electric Retail Rate Authorities (“RERRA”) have
in determining the necessary level of Resource Adequacy and works in concert with LSEs, as LSEs
are the entities responsible for providing demand forecasts that help drive the development of local
and regional requirements by MISO. Additionally, MISO partners with the Organization of MISO
States, Inc. (“OMS”) to conduct a survey (“OMS-MISO Survey”) of resource owners within MISO
footprint on an annual basis to assess anticipated generating capacity over a five-year planning
horizon. The OMS-MISO Survey results, along with MISO’s Planning Resource Auction
(“PRA”) and other forward-looking analyses (e.g., Futures), provide a comprehensive view of
system risks and resource needs, supporting states in their resource adequacy responsibilities and
members in their resource planning.

                 2.      The MISO region is expected to experience capacity surpluses in the
                         near term.

                         a.       OMS-MISO Survey

        The OMS-MISO Survey provides transparency in expectations of future resource adequacy
plans, among other vehicles.4 Overall, the OMS–MISO Survey provides a five-year view of
resource adequacy, indicating if expected capacity based on member plans will meet planning
reserve margins and yield a surplus or deficit.

        The 2026 OMS-MISO Survey results, published on June 4, 2026, show an adaptive
response to increasing demand through generation additions that sustain near-term resource
adequacy.5 As provided in the 2026 OMS-MISO Survey results, the MISO region is projected to
maintain sufficient capacity to meet demand across the next five years, based upon current load
forecasts and anticipated load growth.6 MISO examines the survey results in tandem with forecast
data submitted by LSEs. The forecast data indicates that Load growth as submitted by LSEs
continues to accelerate, with a Compound Annual Growth Rate (“CAGR”) projected between
3.1% and 5.1% over five years.7 The study results also indicates that, to support rising demand,
the MISO Region needs to maintain the increased pace of capacity additions, noting that timely
generation builds, generator interconnection queue improvements, as well as the Expedited
Resource Adequacy Study (“ERAS”), will help meet this need.8 The study results further confirm
that seasonal reliability risk is changing in a way that contributes to shifting hours of reliability

                         b.      MISO’s Regional Resource Assessment

       MISO is confident that the MISO Region will continue to be resource adequate in both the
near and longer term. In addition to the OMS-MISO Survey, MISO had also developed Regional
Resource Assessment (“RRA”) to assess the state of resource adequacy in its footprint in the past.
The RRA10 was one of the periodic studies MISO used to forecast how the mix of electricity-
generating resources in the MISO Region could evolve going forward.

        While the RRA and the OMS-MISO Survey are similar in some ways, there are some key
differences. The RRA is a 20-year outlook based on publicly announced resource plans and state
and policy goals, whereas the OMS-MISO Survey is a more near-term (5-year outlook) resource
adequacy assessment based on member plans and resource addition trends. Separately but related,
MISO also develops MISO Futures which typically entails two or more scenarios, with 20-year
outlook, and is used for transmission planning purposes.

           B.    MISO’s Efforts to Support Resource Adequacy

        MISO works diligently to develop, implement, and refine programs to give states and our
members the support needed to ensure resource adequacy in the MISO Region. MISO’s ongoing
resource adequacy efforts involve a holistic, stakeholder-driven approach that has culminated in
numerous Tariff enhancements, some of which are under development and some of which have
recently taken effect. This filing discusses the subset of those initiatives that specifically address
the market reforms to send transparent price signals that provide all parties with the information
necessary to make informed decisions in their resource planning efforts. These initiatives are
discussed in greater detail in the remainder of this section. MISO anticipates that it will provide
more detail on additional initiatives addressing other aspects of the large load integration challenge
in a forthcoming abeyance request.

                 1.      Seasonal Construct and Reliability Based Demand Curve

         MISO’s recent shift to a seasonal capacity market with seasonal accredited capacity better
reflects extreme weather conditions that have become more prevalent. These weather conditions
affect both the seasonal peak demand and the available seasonal supply. In addition, the seasonal
construct better reflects the seasonal planned & forced outage patterns of supply. The recent
implementation of the Reliability Based Demand Curve (“RBDC”) reflects the contributions to
reliability incremental MWs can add to the system. The RBDC helps with price signals by
indicating if the MISO Region has sufficient capacity for the prompt Planning Year. On the supply

seasons (Schedule 53, seasonal accredited capacity resources).

        Data from the 2025-2026 PRA confirm the reliability benefits of the RBDC construct. At
a system level, MISO cleared more capacity beyond the seasonal PRM. The auction cleared above
seasonal final reliability target, representing additional reliability value at cost competitive prices.
For all seasons, Subregional RBDCs set the requirement for both subregions. The efficiency of
the RBDC enabled MISO to secure more capacity at a significantly lower price.

                  2.       Transition to the Direct Loss-of-Load Accreditation Methodology

         MISO is currently transitioning to a two-step accreditation approach (the “Direct Loss-of-
Load” or “DLOL”-based methodology) that accredits capacity based on marginal contribution to
reliability during periods of highest system risk (“marginal effective load carrying capability” or
“marginal ELCC”) on a Resource Class basis. MISO’s DLOL-based methodology combines both
probabilistic and deterministic elements into a single resource accreditation process. Simply
described, the DLOL-based methodology takes two steps by first determining the size of the pie,
and second, divvying up the pie. The DLOL-based accreditation methodology will provide both
MISO members and regulators engaged in integrated resource planning the right investment and
retirement signals to help ensure the availability of resources with the attributes necessary to
maintain reliability into the future.

                  3.       Expedited Resource Addition Study

         In June of 2025, consistent with the Commission’s direction, MISO filed its revised
Expedited Resource Addition Study (“ERAS”) proposal (“Revised ERAS Proposal”). As noted
in its filing, the ERAS proposal was driven by the fact that MISO was facing urgent near-term
resource adequacy and reliability concerns due to load growth, generation retirement, and delays
in the interconnection process11 and that it would experience a 4.7 gigawatt (GW) shortfall by 2028
if currently planned generation facility retirements were to occur.12

        In support of the ERAS proposal MISO asserted that, while it has undertaken reforms to
improve queue processing, the current processing presents a barrier to developing generation that
can address these near-term needs. As such, MISO proposed revisions to its Generator
Interconnection Procedures (“GIP”) and pro forma Generator Interconnection Agreement (“GIA”)
to establish a ERAS process, which provides for accelerated study of interconnection requests that
will address urgent resource adequacy and reliability needs in the near term (i.e., within the next
five years).13 Specifically, under the Revised ERAS Proposal, MISO proposed to create a quarterly

       The Commission accepted MISO’s ERAS proposal on July 21, 2025, finding that MISO’s
proposed Tariff revisions accomplish the purposes of the Commission’s final rules on generator
interconnection, including Order Nos. 2003 and 2023, by helping to ensure that interconnection

and timely manner.15

         ERAS was filed as short term, limited-use, ‘bridge’ process to enable generators needed to
respond to specifically identified and urgent resource adequacy and reliability needs, thus giving
MISO’s broader queue reforms time to take effect. ERAS has succeeded in its goals. To date, 40
projects and 19 GWs of generation have completed the accelerated ERAS process and received
final or near-final generator interconnection agreements allowing them to meet these urgent needs.
MISO has filled the 50 Load-Serving Entity (“LSE”) slots and 10 Independent Power Producer
(“IPP”) slots and expects to fill the remaining 8 retail choice spots allowed under the ERAS caps
prior to the ERAS sunset date. However, while ERAS has been extremely useful and necessary
in the short term, MISO acknowledges that it is not permanent and that other new processes or
enhancements to existing processes must address longer-term needs.

                  4.       Improving Queue Speed

        MISO has also made reforms that, taken collectively, enable it to become an industry leader
in facing the challenges of a swelling interconnection queue while addressing both the current and
projected needs of Interconnection Customers and load for a more reliable and efficient
transmission system and Tariff processes tailored to meet emerging needs.

        In January 2017, MISO comprehensively restructured the GIP and instituted a three-phase
Definitive Planning Phase (“DPP”) process16 to facilitate a structured study and restudy of
proposed generation projects (“2017 Queue Reform”).17 The key elements of the novel GIP

         After the implementation of the 2017 Queue Reform, MISO and its stakeholders continued
to evaluate the effectiveness of the new three-phase DPP process, responding to emerging issues
and refining the initial design with various improvements, both internally and through FERC
filings. The following additional main improvements to the three-phase DPP process were
implemented: (1) reforms to strengthen certain milestone and site control requirements (2019);20
(2) reforms to the Option to Build, harm test calculation, and provisional GIA requirements
(2021);21 (3) reforms to classify fuel type change requests made in the DPP process as a Material
Modification and allow Interconnection Customers to request Surplus Interconnection Service
earlier in the interconnection study process (2021);22 (4) and an innovative proposal to reduce the
GIP timeline by offering enhanced flexibility and an optional path for Interconnection Customers
to execute GIAs in under one year, thereby improving coordination and alignment with MISO’s
transmission expansion planning process, and to implement various other enhancements to the
interconnection process (2022).23

        In 2023, during the pendency of the Order No. 2023 process, MISO embarked on yet
another reform to strengthen its withdrawal penalty regime, including through the adoption of an
Automatic Withdrawal Penalty, and further refine its site control requirements. As MISO
explained in its filing, the reforms were critical to address the ballooning size of MISO’s generator
interconnection queue and winnow out the speculative interconnection requests that so frequently
distort price signals and delay cost certainty to the developers of generation. The Commission
found these reforms just and reasonable and accepted them effective January 22, 2024,24 to apply
starting from MISO’s DPP-2024 queue cycle.

       In addition, MISO worked with its RTO neighbors, PJM Interconnection, LLC (“PJM”)
and Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”), to improve affected system studies procedures and
requirements that are contained in MISO’s Joint Operating Agreements (“JOAs”) with these

         MISO continues to work with its state commissions, stakeholders, and neighbors to
improve the efficiency, accuracy, and speed of its interconnection queue through developing
innovative solutions. For example, MISO integrated modeling software Suite of Unified Grid
Analyses with Renewables (“SUGAR”), for Phase 1 DPP studies with plans to integrate in Phase
2 and 3. SUGAR is designed to perform power flow analyses, identify Network Upgrades, allocate
costs using MISO’s Transmission Cost Estimation Guide and Transmission Owner upgrade inputs,
and validate constraint mitigation. The SUGAR software leverages powerful circuit simulation
methods developed to study billion-transistor electronic systems; this innovation underlies the
ability to expedite some of the more time-consuming aspects of running interconnection studies.
In addition to providing data within MISO’s acceptable tolerances, as benchmarked against current
software, SUGAR reduced DPP phase 1 cycle time significantly from the status quo as evidenced
in the DPP 2022, 2023 and 2025 cycles. The implementation of SUGAR advances MISO’s
Reliability Imperative by continuing to improve processes for new generator interconnections.

                 5.       Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue Study

        The MISO-SPP Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue Study (“JTIQ”) has sped the queue
up considerably by providing an alternative to the backlogged ordinary affected systems study
process with SPP while providing both more efficient solutions to the needs of multiple cycles of
Interconnection Customers as well as greater up-front cost certainty regarding potentially
significant affected systems costs to generators entering the Definitive Planning Phase or MISO’s
ERAS processes. This increased efficiency and cost certainty allows generators to reach GIA
faster and develop their projects from a starting point of increased cost certainty.

        The JTIQ portfolio directly enables new generation to serve emerging load by proactively
constructing the transmission backbone needed for interconnection, rather than waiting for
incremental upgrades triggered by one project at a time. By identifying and mitigating cross‑seam
constraints in advance, JTIQ provides large, regionally optimized transmission solutions that
unlock more than 28 GW of new interconnection capability along the MISO‑SPP seam. Because
these upgrades are included upfront in MISO and SPP’s planning and interconnection models
inclusive of ERAS studies, DPP cycles, and Expedited Project Reviews; projects can interconnect
faster and with far greater cost certainty.

         C.      MISO’s Future Efforts to Bring Resources Online Faster

                 1.       Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement – Expected

       MISO began working with stakeholders in 2025 to develop a more robust zero injection
generator interconnection agreement (“ZGIA”) to facilitate faster interconnection of generation
resources that will be co-located with load and will not inject energy further onto the Transmission
System. The ZGIA provides a limited, structured option to support large load integration through:

           •   A limited service framework supported by associated generation,
           •   Defined interconnection study processes tailored to zero-injection configurations,
               and,
           •   Clear allocation of operational and planning responsibilities.

        This construct enables a pathway for certain large load configurations to achieve speed to
reliable power while maintaining system reliability. A table of MISO’s stakeholder meetings and
links to respective materials regarding MISO’s ZGIA proposal is provided in Attachment A hereto.
MISO expects to submit the ZGIA proposal to the Commission in a Federal Power Act Section
205 filing on, or about July 31, 2026.

               2.      Large Load Parallel Study Process

        Current load and generation study processes are dependent on each other, requiring one to
be complete before the next can begin. Some large load customers are seeking a more integrated,
predictable experience that reflects the real-world pairing of large loads with the generation needed
to serve it, without requiring co-location. MISO is working to address these concerns through the
proposed Large Load Parallel Study Process. The Large Load Parallel Study Process will be used
for studying load greater than or equal to 250MW and will allow MISO to integrate studies for
planned load and generation to increase speed to approval and optimize network upgrades.

         Through the proposed Large Load Parallel Study Process, an LSE will submit a proposed
generation and load combination. The generation and load have separate eligibility requirements
(e.g., load ≥250 MW, generation nameplate max 150% of identified load need). The proposed
Large Load Parallel Study Process will analyze generation and transmission using the same study
assumptions applied in Generator Interconnection and MTEP. Both studies will be run
concurrently and in parallel, with the load/transmission model incorporating the planned
generation and planned load and finish at approximately the same time—within 120 days. The
proposed process is intended to ensure faster and more transparent interconnection arrangements
for large loads, while offering customers speed-to-power, optimized transmission solutions, and
greater certainty to support siting, financing, and state coordination. This solution aligns with the
spirit of the Commission’s Show Cause Order for interconnection process arrangements to address
the speed of adding generation to serve large load. The outcome of the processes is MTEP
approval of transmission required to reliably facilitate the withdrawal of the load and injection
rights for the generation.

        MISO initiated the stakeholder process with a presentation of the Large Load Parallel Study
Process at the July 16, 2026, Large Load Working Group and has requested stakeholder feedback
on the proposed process. MISO will continue stakeholder discussions on the Large Load Parallel

representatives of Transmission Owners and non-Transmission Owners, as well as all state
commissions within the MISO Region and the Organization of MISO States. The filing has been
posted electronically on MISO’s website at https://www.misoenergy.org/legal/ferc-filings/ for
other interested parties in this matter.

VI.    CONCLUSION

         For all of the foregoing reasons, MISO respectfully requests that the Commission accept
this filing in compliance with the requirements of the Show Cause Order and grant waiver of any
Commission regulations the Commission deems applicable to this filing in order for the
Commission to accept it as proposed. The MISO region currently is resource adequate and MISO’s
work with recent reforms and partnership with OMS, the states and members has provided a firm
foundation. However, with new urgent challenges created by the introduction of new large spot
loads, additional tools are needed to support this growth and maintain Resource Adequacy going
forward. MISO looks forward to bringing new Resource Adequacy tools to LSEs to meet the
unique challenges associated with the new spot load growth occurring across the footprint. These
tools will help support affordability for customers while enabling speed to power in a reliable cost
effective manner that can meet the new emerging demand.
